prompt: Your indicators have failed and you need to show that you are turning left. Which hand signal do you give?
options: Right arm out of the window with the forearm bent down, circling anti-clockwise
Left arm straight out of the window, level with the shoulder, palm facing forward
Right arm out of the window with the forearm bent up, palm facing forward
explanation: All three K53 hand signals are given with the right arm, so it is the shape of the arm that carries the meaning: forearm down and circling means left. A left arm out of the window is not a recognised signal at all, and the right arm bent upwards means you are slowing down or stopping.

prompt: The driver in front of you puts their right arm out of the window with the forearm bent upwards and the palm facing forward. What are they telling you?
options: They are about to turn right
They are about to turn left
They are slowing down or about to stop
explanation: Forearm bent up with the palm forward is the signal for slowing or stopping, so you should increase your following distance and be ready to brake. A right turn is signalled with the arm held straight out level with the shoulder, and a left turn with the forearm bent down and circling anti-clockwise.

prompt: An ambulance comes up behind you sounding its siren and showing its emergency identification lamp. What must you do?
options: Hold your position, because a vehicle already on the road keeps its right of way
Give it immediate and absolute right of way, moving to the left as soon as you safely can
Speed up and stay ahead of it until you reach a turnoff where you can leave the road
explanation: The law gives a siren or emergency lamp immediate and absolute right of way, so the road must open for it. You never keep your right of way against a siren, and speeding up to stay ahead only holds the emergency vehicle back and puts you over the limit.

prompt: You are driving in the right-hand lane of a two-lane road when a fire engine appears behind you with its siren on. What is the correct way to respond?
options: Work out where it is coming from, indicate, and move to the left as soon as it is safe, stopping and waiting if you have to
Brake hard and stop where you are so that it can decide how to get past you
Keep your speed and lane, because moving over could cause a crash with the traffic on your left
explanation: You must clear the path deliberately: identify where the vehicle is coming from, signal, and move left as soon as it is safe, then carry on once it has passed. Stopping dead in a live lane leaves you blocking the road, and staying put is exactly what the immediate-and-absolute rule forbids.

prompt: You have a green light at an intersection when an ambulance with its siren on approaches from your left, against its red light. What must you do?
options: Carry on through, because a green light gives you right of way over other traffic
Hoot to warn the ambulance that you are the one with right of way
Give way immediately and let it through, even though your light is green
explanation: Emergency drivers are allowed to pass signs and signals that would otherwise hold them back, and your duty to give way is immediate and absolute, so the green light does not protect you here. Driving on or hooting both assume a right of way that a siren cancels.

prompt: You are involved in an accident in which a passenger is injured, and you did not give your details to a traffic officer at the scene. By when must you report the accident at a police station?
options: As soon as you reasonably can, and in any case within 24 hours
Within 48 hours
Within 7 days
explanation: If your details were not given to a traffic officer at the scene, you must report at a police station as soon as you reasonably can and within 24 hours, taking your driving licence and ID number. The 48-hour and 7-day options are simply longer than the law allows and would leave you in breach of your duty.

prompt: After a crash in which someone was hurt, you are shaken and a bystander offers you a drink to calm your nerves. What does the law say?
options: It is allowed once the ambulance has taken the injured person away
You may not drink alcohol or take a narcotic drug before you have reported the accident and, if an officer asks for it, been medically examined
It is allowed as long as you are not going to drive again that day
explanation: Drinking after an accident is barred until you have reported it and submitted to a medical examination if an officer requires one, because alcohol taken afterwards destroys the evidence of your state at the time of the crash. Neither the ambulance leaving nor your decision not to drive again lifts that duty.

prompt: You are approaching an intersection where you intend to turn left. Where must your vehicle be positioned?
options: As near to the left of the roadway as conditions allow, having signalled before you get there
In the middle of your side of the road, so you have room to swing wide into the side street
Just left of the centre line, so following traffic can pass you on the left
explanation: A left turn is made from as near the left of the roadway as conditions allow, with the signal given before you reach the intersection. Sitting in the middle or near the centre line invites traffic up your left-hand side and is exactly the drifting position examiners penalise.

prompt: You are going to turn right at an intersection on an ordinary two-way road. Where should you position your vehicle before the turn?
options: Hard against the right-hand kerb of the road
In the centre of your lane, turning from wherever the lane happens to be
As near as you can get to just left of the middle of the road
explanation: For a right turn on a two-way road you move as close as conditions allow to just left of the middle of the road, which keeps you on your own half while leaving room for traffic to pass on your left. Hugging the right-hand kerb puts you into oncoming traffic, and simply staying centred in your lane blocks the drivers behind you.

prompt: You are correctly positioned and signalling to turn right, but oncoming traffic is steady. When may you begin the turn?
options: As soon as the first oncoming driver has to slow down for you, because you are already committed
Only when there is a gap big enough for you to complete the turn without obstructing or endangering other traffic
Immediately, provided you keep your indicator on throughout the turn
explanation: You may not start a right turn unless you can finish it without obstructing or endangering anyone, so you wait in position for a real gap. Forcing oncoming drivers to brake and relying on your indicator to excuse the move are both the same mistake: an indicator asks for space, it does not grant it.

prompt: You are travelling on a one-way street and want to turn right at the next intersection. Where must you position your vehicle?
options: As near as you can to the right-hand side of the roadway
Just left of the middle of the roadway, as you would on a two-way road
In whichever lane is emptiest, since a one-way street has no oncoming traffic
explanation: On a one-way street the whole roadway is yours to use in one direction, so a right turn is made from as near the right-hand side as you can get. Taking up the middle position needlessly blocks traffic that could pass on your left, and picking the emptiest lane ignores the positioning rule the examiner is marking.

prompt: You are turning right at an intersection on a two-way road. At what point may you cross into the right-hand half of the road?
options: As soon as you have signalled, so that you are lined up well before the intersection
Only once you are inside the intersection itself, keeping left of any traffic island
Once the vehicle in front of you has cleared the intersection
explanation: You stay on your own half of the road up to the intersection and only cross into the right half inside the intersection, passing left of any traffic island. Cutting across early puts you on the wrong side of the road facing oncoming traffic, and the movement of the car ahead of you has nothing to do with where the right half of the road begins.
